method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Recognising and managing anaphylaxis is the most important consideration** in any child with suspected food allergy.
claims.source_text: Recognition and management of anaphylaxis is the most important consideration in any child presenting with suspected food allergy
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **IgE-mediated reactions usually start within 60 minutes of ingestion.** Commonest foods: peanut, tree nuts, shellfish, fish, milk, egg, wheat, soy, sesame.
claims.source_text: IgE-mediated reactions are characterized by stereotypical signs and symptoms that develop usually within 60 minutes of ingestion … The commonest foods implicated in IgE-mediated allergy are peanut, tree nuts, shellfish, fish, milk, egg, wheat, soy, and sesame
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Anaphylaxis = any acute respiratory and/or cardiovascular symptoms, even without skin signs.** Mild-to-moderate reactions involve only skin and/or gut.
claims.source_text: Anaphylaxis is any acute onset of respiratory and/or cardiovascular symptoms, even if skin symptoms are not present, and may be life threatening … Mild to moderate allergic reactions may involve only skin and/or gastrointestinal symptoms
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Respiratory:** hoarse voice, throat tightness, difficulty swallowing, stridor, wheeze, persistent cough. **Cardiovascular:** pallor, dizziness, collapse.
claims.source_text: Respiratory: Hoarse voice, tightness in throat, difficulty swallowing, stridor Wheeze, chest tightness, difficulty breathing, persistent coughing Cardiovascular: Pallor Dizziness, collapse
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Risk factors:** personal atopy (asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis) · atopy or food allergy in parents or siblings · other IgE-mediated food allergies.
claims.source_text: Personal history of atopy (asthma, eczema or allergic rhinitis) History of atopy or food allergy in parents or siblings Known other IgE-mediated food allergies
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A contact reaction around the mouth is common in eczema and is not diagnostic** of IgE-mediated allergy; nor is eczema alone.
claims.source_text: Contact skin reaction – erythema and/or urticaria occurring on any areas of skin in contact with the food, more commonly around a child’s mouth. Common in children with eczema and not diagnostic of IgE-mediated food allergy … Eczema – eczema alone is not indicative of an immediate IgE-mediated food allergy
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **FPIES is non-IgE:** profuse vomiting ± diarrhoea two to four hours after a recently introduced food, sometimes with pallor, poor tone, hypothermia and low blood pressure.
claims.source_text: Food Protein Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome (FPIES) – profuse vomiting +/- diarrhoea occurring two to four hours after ingestion of a recently-introduced food. Sometimes associated with pallor, poor tone, a drop in body temperature and low blood pressure. FPIES is non-IgE mediated
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Do not test in the acute setting.** Diagnosis needs a convincing history, supported by skin prick testing or specific IgE done after the event.
claims.source_text: Investigations for food allergy are neither necessary nor interpretable in the acute setting … Diagnosis of food allergy requires convincing history and is supported by Skin Prick Testing (SPT) and specific IgE tests, both of which can be performed after the event
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Skin prick testing is preferred, by a paediatric allergy-trained clinician only**; otherwise targeted serum specific IgE for the suspected trigger(s) only.
claims.source_text: Skin Prick Testing (SPT) is preferred for suspected IgE allergy, but should only be performed by a paediatric allergy-trained clinician … If there is no access to an allergy-trained clinician, serum specific IgE testing may be performed. Targeted testing for only the specific suspected food trigger(s) is recommended
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **No screening panels and no testing for foods not yet eaten** — they drive unnecessary avoidance and more future allergy. **No allergy testing for non-IgE allergy** (non-IgE cow's milk allergy, FPIES).
claims.source_text: Food allergen screening panels or screening for foods a child has not yet ingested are not recommended, as this can lead to unnecessary food allergen avoidance and greater risk of future food allergies … Allergy testing is not necessary and is not indicated for suspected non IgE-mediated food allergies, eg non-IgE cow-milk allergy and FPIES
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline immediately, 10 microgram/kg or 0.01 mL/kg of 1:1000 (max 0.5 mL); repeat after 5 minutes if not improving.**
claims.source_text: If severe allergic reaction to food, consistent with anaphylaxis: Immediately administer Intramuscular Adrenaline, 10 microgram/kg or 0.01 mL/kg of 1:1000 (maximum 0.5 mL) Repeat after 5 minutes if not improving
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Mild-to-moderate: non-sedating antihistamine, e.g. cetirizine orally** — 1–2 years 2.5 mg · 2–6 years 5 mg · 6 years and above 10 mg; safe from 6 months at 0.25 mg/kg/dose.
claims.source_text: If mild-moderate allergic to reaction, administer a non-sedative antihistamine, eg: Cetirizine: 1–2 years – 2.5 mg oral 2–6 years – 5 mg oral 6 years and above – 10 mg oral … Note: cetirizine has been shown to be safe in infants from 6 months of age (0.25 mg/kg/dose)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Or loratadine orally once daily:** 1–2 years 2.5 mg · over 2 years and under 30 kg 5 mg · over 30 kg 10 mg.
claims.source_text: Loratadine: 1–2 years, oral 2.5 mg once daily >2 years and <30 kg, oral 5 mg once daily >30 kg, oral 10 mg once daily
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Observe until symptoms are not escalating**, then discharge with a plan.
claims.source_text: Observe to make sure symptoms do not escalate, then discharge with plan below
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A child must avoid the suspected food, but not similar foods already tolerated.** Teach label reading.
claims.source_text: A child must avoid food(s) suspected of causing an IgE-mediated reaction, but not similar foods that have previously been tolerated … Strict avoidance of suspected food allergen(s): requires parental education on reading ingredient labels
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Tree nuts travel in pairs:** walnut ↔ pecan, cashew ↔ pistachio — avoid both.
claims.source_text: if reacted to walnuts, avoid pecans and vice-versa if reacted to cashews, avoid pistachios and vice-versa
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Give an ASCIA action plan even before the food is confirmed:** red (anaphylaxis) plan after a severe reaction, green (allergy) plan after a mild-to-moderate one.
claims.source_text: A child presenting with suspected food allergy should go home with an allergy action plan and appropriate follow-up … Allergy action plan: (Give plan even if food not yet confirmed by investigation) History of severe reaction/anaphylaxis (ASCIA anaphylaxis red plan): History of mild-to-moderate allergic food reaction (ASCIA allergy green plan):
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Keep a varied diet, including previously tolerated allergenic foods, eaten regularly.** Refer to a dietitian if many or staple foods are being cut.
claims.source_text: Ensure child continues to eat a varied diet, which includes other allergenic foods/nuts that were previously tolerated on a regular basis. … consider dietician referral if many foods being eliminated, especially if staple foods (eg wheat, milk)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Discuss with the paediatric or allergy team:** any suspected or proven food anaphylaxis · suspected allergy with unstable asthma · unclear trigger or equivocal tests · multiple food allergies · suspected tolerance that may need an oral food challenge.
claims.source_text: Consider consultation with local paediatric/allergy team when Any child with suspected or proven anaphylaxis to a food Child with suspected allergy and unstable asthma Unclear food trigger or equivocal investigations Multiple food allergies Suspected tolerance to food on follow-up and which may require an Oral Food Challenge
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Adrenaline auto-injectors** (usually a 12-month expiry; GP can re-prescribe): **150 mcg under 20 kg · 300 mcg from 20 kg · 300–500 mcg close to or above 50 kg.**
claims.source_text: Adrenaline auto-injectors usually have a 12-month expiry, and ongoing prescriptions can be done via local GP 150 mcg if child is under 20 kg 300 mcg once child is 20 kg 300-500 mcg if child close to 50 kg or above
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Identify and manage asthma — poorly controlled asthma is a risk factor for fatal anaphylaxis.** Re-check action-plan knowledge and auto-injector technique regularly.
claims.source_text: Identify and manage any asthma. Poorly controlled asthma is a risk factor for fatal anaphylaxis … Regular education on allergy management plan, including checking adrenaline auto-injector technique if child has anaphylaxis plan
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Food allergy - IgE mediated food allergy' (Last updated October 2021), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Food_allergy_-_IgE_mediated_food_allergy/, retrieved 2026-09-23
